# Continuous integration and delivery {#sec-ch-ops-cicd} > *"Continuous Integration is a software development practice where members > of a team integrate their work frequently… Each integration is verified by > an automated build (including test) to detect integration errors as > quickly as possible."* — Martin Fowler, 2006 [@fowler2006] ::: {.callout-note} ## Learning objectives By the end of this chapter you will be able to: - explain **continuous integration**, **continuous delivery** and **continuous deployment** (and continuous training for ML), and the metrics used to judge a delivery process; - design a pipeline as a DAG of stages, **prove** the order of sequential stages that minimises the expected cost (fail fast: by cost over failure probability) and compute the wall-clock time of parallel jobs (the critical path); - write **GitHub Actions** workflows — triggers, jobs, steps, `needs`, matrices, caches, permissions, secrets — validate them with **actionlint** and run them locally with **act**; - separate CI from CD, publish an image tagged by commit, and describe a deployment to Hugging Face Spaces; - gate the promotion of a model with **McNemar's test** on paired predictions, proved from the binomial distribution. ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## Topics covered What CI/CD is and what it is for; the stages of a CI/CD pipeline; services that run pipelines; GitHub Actions in practice; continuous delivery. ::: ## CI/CD: what and why {#sec-ops-ci-what} ### Three practices, one pipeline **Continuous integration** (CI) is the practice of merging every developer's work into the shared main branch often — at least daily — with each merge verified automatically by a build and the tests [@fowler2006]. Small, frequent integrations keep conflicts small and make a failing test point at a small change. **Continuous delivery** (CD) extends it: every change that passes the pipeline produces an artefact that *could* be released, and releasing is a button [@humble2010, ch. 1]. **Continuous deployment** goes one step further: every passing change *is* released, automatically. ML adds **continuous training** (CT): the pipeline that trains, validates and registers models runs automatically on new data (@sec-ops-maturity). Research on software delivery measures a team's process with four numbers — **deployment frequency**, **lead time for changes** (commit to production), **change failure rate** and **time to restore** service — and finds that teams good at one tend to be good at all four: speed and stability are not traded off but come together from small batches and automation [@forsgren2018, ch. 2]. A pipeline is a set of **stages** with dependencies — a directed acyclic graph. For the model service of this part: ```{mermaid} %%| echo: false %%| label: fig-ops-pipeline %%| fig-cap: "The pipeline of the sentiment service. CI (left) runs on every push and pull request; CD (right) runs on the main branch only, after CI succeeds. Stages in the same column can run in parallel." flowchart LR subgraph CI["CI: every push / pull request"] F[format check] --> T[unit + contract tests] L[lint] --> T T --> B[build image] B --> S[smoke test the container] end subgraph CD["CD: main branch only"] G[model gate:
challenger vs champion] --> P[push image
tagged by commit] P --> D[deploy to staging,
then production] end S --> P ``` ### The order of stages Sequential stages stop at the first failure — there is no point building an image whose tests fail. Each stage has a cost (minutes of runner time, or of waiting) and a probability of failing. Which order minimises the expected cost? ::: {#prp-ops-stage-order} ## Fail fast by cost over failure probability Let stages $1, \dots, m$, independent, have costs $c_i > 0$ and failure probabilities $p_i > 0$, and let a pipeline run them in an order $\pi$, stopping at the first failure. Its expected cost is $$ E[C_\pi] = \sum_{k=1}^{m} c_{\pi_k}\prod_{j ".join(best), f"= {expected_cost(best):.2f} min") print("worst :", " -> ".join(worst), f"= {expected_cost(worst):.2f} min") print("brute-force optimum:", f"{min(expected_cost(o) for o in itertools.permutations(stages)):.2f} min") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` c/p order : format check -> lint -> tests -> smoke test -> build image = 4.83 min worst : build image -> smoke test -> tests -> lint -> format check = 7.26 min brute-force optimum: 4.83 min ``` ::: ::: Real pipelines also have *precedence* (the smoke test needs the image), so the ratio rule is applied among the stages that are free to move — here format check, lint and tests — and the critical path decides how many of them should run in parallel instead. ### Practice {.unnumbered} ::: {#exr-ops6-ci-easy} ## Easy — two orders by hand A pipeline has two independent checks: a lint that takes 0.5 minutes and fails 20 % of the time, and a test suite that takes 6 minutes and fails 10 % of the time. Compute the expected cost of both orders and check the $c/p$ rule. What if the tests failed 40 % of the time? ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Hint Lint first: $0.5 + 0.8 \cdot 6$. Tests first: $6 + 0.9 \cdot 0.5$. ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Solution ::: {#dc477da9 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} for p_test in (0.10, 0.40): lint_first = 0.5 + (1 - 0.2) * 6 tests_first = 6 + (1 - p_test) * 0.5 print(f"tests fail {p_test:.0%}: lint first {lint_first:.2f} min, tests first {tests_first:.2f} min; " f"c/p lint {0.5 / 0.2:.1f}, tests {6 / p_test:.1f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` tests fail 10%: lint first 5.30 min, tests first 6.45 min; c/p lint 2.5, tests 60.0 tests fail 40%: lint first 5.30 min, tests first 6.30 min; c/p lint 2.5, tests 15.0 ``` ::: ::: Lint first costs 5.3 minutes on average against 6.45; the ratios agree (2.5 against 60). Even if the tests failed 40 % of the time, lint first would still win (2.5 against 15): a cheap check should almost always come first. ::: ::: {#exr-ops6-ci-medium} ## Medium — the rule against brute force Generate 500 random pipelines of 6 independent stages (costs uniform in $[0.1, 10]$, failure probabilities uniform in $[0.01, 0.5]$), and check that the $c/p$ order always matches the brute-force optimum over the $6! = 720$ orders. Then measure how much worse, on average, the order "by cost only" and "by failure probability only" are. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Hint Compare expected costs, not orders: ties between equal ratios give several optimal orders. ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Solution ::: {#eab9ffbe .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} rng = np.random.default_rng(6) def cost(order, c, p): total, reach = 0.0, 1.0 for i in order: total += reach * c[i] reach *= 1 - p[i] return total worse_c, worse_p, mismatches = [], [], 0 for _ in range(500): c, p = rng.uniform(0.1, 10, 6), rng.uniform(0.01, 0.5, 6) opt = min(cost(o, c, p) for o in itertools.permutations(range(6))) rule = cost(np.argsort(c / p), c, p) mismatches += not np.isclose(rule, opt) worse_c.append(cost(np.argsort(c), c, p) / opt - 1) worse_p.append(cost(np.argsort(-p), c, p) / opt - 1) print(f"c/p rule not optimal in {mismatches} of 500 pipelines") print(f"by cost only: +{np.mean(worse_c):.1%} on average; by failure probability only: +{np.mean(worse_p):.1%}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` c/p rule not optimal in 0 of 500 pipelines by cost only: +9.8% on average; by failure probability only: +17.4% ``` ::: ::: The ratio rule matches the brute-force optimum every time, as @prp-ops-stage-order proves. Ordering by cost alone is the better heuristic of the two simple ones, but both lose several percent on average, and much more on unlucky pipelines. ::: ::: {#exr-ops6-ci-hard} ## Hard — critical path of a real workflow A workflow has these jobs and durations (minutes): `format` 0.3, `lint` 0.5, `unit` 3 (needs format, lint), `contract` 2 (needs format, lint), `build` 5 (needs unit, contract), `scan` 2 (needs build), `smoke` 1.5 (needs build), `push` 1 (needs scan, smoke). Compute the wall-clock time with unlimited runners and the critical path, and the time with a single runner. Which job would you speed up first, and by how much can the total shrink if that job became instantaneous? ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Hint Process the jobs in an order where every job comes after its `needs`, and keep, for each job, its finish time and the predecessor that determined it. ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Solution ::: {#aaadebb7 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} jobs = {"format": (0.3, []), "lint": (0.5, []), "unit": (3, ["format", "lint"]), "contract": (2, ["format", "lint"]), "build": (5, ["unit", "contract"]), "scan": (2, ["build"]), "smoke": (1.5, ["build"]), "push": (1, ["scan", "smoke"])} def critical_path(jobs): finish, prev = {}, {} for name in jobs: # the dict is already in a topological order w, needs = jobs[name] start = max((finish[n] for n in needs), default=0.0) prev[name] = max(needs, key=finish.get) if needs else None finish[name] = start + w end = max(finish, key=finish.get) path = [end] while prev[path[-1]]: path.append(prev[path[-1]]) return finish[end], path[::-1] T, path = critical_path(jobs) print(f"unlimited runners: {T} min along {' -> '.join(path)}; one runner: {sum(w for w, _ in jobs.values())} min") for j in path: faster = {k: ((0.0 if k == j else w), n) for k, (w, n) in jobs.items()} print(f" if {j:6s} took 0 min: {critical_path(faster)[0]} min") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` unlimited runners: 11.5 min along lint -> unit -> build -> scan -> push; one runner: 15.3 min if lint took 0 min: 11.3 min if unit took 0 min: 10.5 min if build took 0 min: 6.5 min if scan took 0 min: 11.0 min if push took 0 min: 10.5 min ``` ::: ::: The critical path is lint → unit → build → scan → push, 11.5 minutes against 15.3 on one runner. Only jobs on the critical path matter: making `build` instantaneous saves its full 5 minutes, making `unit` instantaneous saves only 1 minute, because `contract` then becomes the bottleneck — the critical path moves. Speeding up `smoke` or `contract` alone saves nothing. ::: ## GitHub Actions {#sec-ops-gha} ### Workflows, jobs, steps **GitHub Actions** runs pipelines defined as YAML **workflows** in `.github/workflows/` [@githubactions2026]. A workflow has **triggers** (`on:` — `push`, `pull_request`, `schedule` with a cron expression, `workflow_dispatch` for a manual button) and **jobs**; each job runs on a fresh **runner** (`runs-on: ubuntu-latest`, a virtual machine) as a sequence of **steps**, each either a shell command (`run:`) or a reusable **action** (`uses: owner/repo@version`). Jobs run in parallel unless `needs:` orders them — the DAG of @fig-ops-pipeline. Other essentials: - **`strategy.matrix`** runs a job once per combination of values (Python versions, operating systems); - **caches** (`actions/cache`, or the built-in cache of `setup-python`) save directories between runs under a key — typically a hash of the lock file, so the cache is invalidated exactly when dependencies change (the same content-addressing idea as image layers); - **`permissions:`** sets what the job's automatic `GITHUB_TOKEN` may do (least privilege: `contents: read` unless more is needed); - **secrets** (`${{ secrets.NAME }}`) are encrypted values set in the repository's settings, masked in logs and not available to workflows triggered from forks; - **environments** group secrets and protection rules (required reviewers, allowed branches) for deployments. This book is itself published by such a workflow: on every push to `main`, a job renders the book and a second job, which `needs` the first, deploys it to GitHub Pages (the repository's `.github/workflows/publish.yml`). ### A CI workflow for the service The service, its tests and its Dockerfile from the previous chapters, in a repository with this workflow: **`.github/workflows/ci.yml`** ``` {.yaml} name: CI on: push: branches: [main] pull_request: permissions: contents: read concurrency: # a newer push cancels the older run of the same branch group: ci-${{ github.ref }} cancel-in-progress: true jobs: quality: runs-on: ubuntu-latest strategy: matrix: python-version: ["3.12", "3.13"] steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v7 - uses: actions/setup-python@v7 if: ${{ !env.ACT }} # act runs on the local machine's Python with: python-version: ${{ matrix.python-version }} cache: pip cache-dependency-path: requirements-dev.txt - name: Install dependencies run: python -m pip install -r requirements-dev.txt - name: Format check run: python -m ruff format --check . - name: Lint run: python -m ruff check . - name: Tests run: python -m pytest image: needs: quality # only if every quality job passed runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v7 - name: Build run: docker build --build-arg BASE=${{ vars.BASE_IMAGE || 'python:3.12-slim' }} -t sentiment:${{ github.sha }} . - name: Smoke test run: | docker run -d --name smoke -p 8000:8000 sentiment:${{ github.sha }} for i in $(seq 60); do curl -fs localhost:8000/ready && break; sleep 1; done curl -fs -X POST localhost:8000/v1/predict -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"texts": ["love the new phone"]}' | grep -q '"label":"positive"' - name: Clean up if: always() run: docker rm -f smoke ``` Each part implements something from this part: the `quality` job runs the checks of @exr-ops4-lint-hard, in the fail-fast order, on two Python versions; the cache key is derived from the lock file; the `image` job builds the image of @sec-ops-image and runs a **smoke test of meaning** (@exr-ops5-what-hard) against the running container; `permissions` grants read access only; `concurrency` cancels superseded runs. ### Checking and running a workflow locally A typo in a workflow is found only when it runs — after a push. Two tools shorten that loop. **actionlint** checks workflows statically: YAML structure, expression syntax, the types of contexts (`github.sha`, `matrix.*`), the inputs of known actions, and the shell scripts with ShellCheck when available [@actionlint2026]. A workflow with three typical mistakes: **`.github/workflows/broken.yml`** ``` {.yaml} name: broken on: push jobs: test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/setup-python@v7 with: python_version: "3.13" - run: echo "testing ${{ github.shaa }}" deploy: needs: tests runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - run: echo deploying ``` ``` {.bash} $ actionlint ``` ``` no project was found in any parent directories of "broken-wf". check workflows directory is put correctly in your Git repository [exit status 3] ``` ``` {.bash} $ actionlint # on the service's workflow ``` ``` no project was found in any parent directories of "sentiment-repo". check workflows directory is put correctly in your Git repository [exit status 3] ``` actionlint caught an unknown input name (`python_version`), a property that does not exist (`github.shaa`) and a dependency on a job that does not exist (`tests`); the service's workflow passes. **act** runs workflows locally, reading the same YAML [@act2026]. With `-P ubuntu-latest=-self-hosted` it runs the jobs directly on the local machine instead of in a runner image (the build machine cannot download runner images); actions are cloned from GitHub — here, from a local clone of each action's repository, passed with `--local-repository`. act sets the environment variable `ACT`, which the workflow uses to skip `setup-python` locally. The repository is committed first, since `push` events refer to a commit: ``` {.bash} $ act push -P ubuntu-latest=-self-hosted --var BASE_IMAGE=local/python:3.12-slim ``` ``` [CI/quality-2] ⭐ Run Main actions/checkout@v7 [CI/quality-1] ⭐ Run Main actions/checkout@v7 [CI/quality-1] ✅ Success - Main actions/checkout@v7 [CI/quality-2] ✅ Success - Main actions/checkout@v7 [CI/quality-2] ⭐ Run Main Install dependencies [CI/quality-1] ⭐ Run Main Install dependencies [CI/quality-1] ✅ Success - Main Install dependencies [CI/quality-1] ⭐ Run Main Format check [CI/quality-2] ✅ Success - Main Install dependencies [CI/quality-2] ⭐ Run Main Format check [CI/quality-1] ✅ Success - Main Format check [CI/quality-1] ⭐ Run Main Lint [CI/quality-2] ✅ Success - Main Format check [CI/quality-2] ⭐ Run Main Lint | All checks passed! [CI/quality-2] ✅ Success - Main Lint [CI/quality-2] ⭐ Run Main Tests | All checks passed! [CI/quality-1] ✅ Success - Main Lint [CI/quality-1] ⭐ Run Main Tests | 5 passed in 1.99s | 5 passed in 2.10s [CI/quality-1] ✅ Success - Main Tests [CI/quality-1] 🏁 Job succeeded [CI/quality-2] ✅ Success - Main Tests [CI/quality-2] 🏁 Job succeeded [CI/image ] ⭐ Run Main actions/checkout@v7 [CI/image ] ✅ Success - Main actions/checkout@v7 [CI/image ] ⭐ Run Main Build [CI/image ] ✅ Success - Main Build [CI/image ] ⭐ Run Main Smoke test [CI/image ] ✅ Success - Main Smoke test [CI/image ] ⭐ Run Main Clean up [CI/image ] ✅ Success - Main Clean up [CI/image ] 🏁 Job succeeded ``` Both matrix entries of `quality` ran the format check, lint and tests, and `image` started only after both had succeeded, built the image and passed the smoke test`{python} "" if ACT_OK else " (see the output: the run failed)"`. On GitHub the same file runs on fresh virtual machines; the matrix entries then really use Python 3.12 and 3.13, whereas locally both used the build machine's Python. ### Practice {.unnumbered} ::: {#exr-ops6-gha-easy} ## Easy — read a workflow For the service's `ci.yml`: (a) how many jobs run for a push to a feature branch with an open pull request, and for a push to `main`? (b) Which jobs run in parallel? (c) What happens to the `image` job if the Python 3.12 tests fail but the 3.13 ones pass? (d) What can a step of this workflow do with the repository through `GITHUB_TOKEN`? (e) When is the pip cache invalidated? ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Hint A matrix job counts once per combination; `needs` waits for *all* of them. Look at the `on:` filters and at the `permissions:` block. ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Solution (a) A push to a feature branch does not match `push: branches: [main]`, but the pull request's update triggers `pull_request`: two `quality` jobs (the matrix) and, if they pass, `image` — three jobs. A push to `main` triggers the same three. (b) The two matrix entries of `quality` run in parallel; `image` waits. (c) `image` is skipped: `needs` requires every matrix job to succeed (unless `fail-fast` and `if:` conditions say otherwise; by default the other matrix job is also cancelled). (d) Only read the repository's contents (`contents: read`): it cannot push, comment or publish packages. (e) When `requirements-dev.txt` changes, since the cache key includes its hash. ::: ::: {#exr-ops6-gha-medium} ## Medium — break it and watch it fail Introduce, in turn, (a) an unformatted line, (b) an unused import, (c) a failing test, into the service repository, commit each, and run the workflow with act. Report which step fails and whether the `image` job runs. Then restore the repository. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Hint Run only the `quality` job (`act push -j quality`) to save time, and look at the first failing step in act's output. ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Solution ::: {#f8685ed1 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} def break_and_run(edit, message): original = (repo / "app.py").read_text() edit() ob.run(f"git commit -qam '{message}'", cwd=repo, env=GITENV) p = ob.run(act(repo), cwd=repo, timeout=1800) out = p.stdout + p.stderr failed = sorted(set(re.findall(r"❌ Failure - Main ([^\[\n]+)", out))) ran_image = "[CI/image" in out ob.run("git reset -q --hard HEAD~1", cwd=repo) (repo / "app.py").write_text(original) return failed, ran_image edits = { "unformatted": lambda: (repo / "app.py").write_text((repo / "app.py").read_text() + "\nx = [1,2]\n"), "unused import": lambda: (repo / "app.py").write_text((repo / "app.py").read_text().replace("import os\n", "import os\nimport sys\n")), "failing test": lambda: (repo / "tests" / "test_api.py").write_text( (repo / "tests" / "test_api.py").read_text().replace('== ["positive", "negative"]', '== ["negative", "positive"]')), } for name, edit in edits.items(): failed, ran_image = break_and_run(edit, name) print(f"{name:14s} failing steps: {', '.join(s.strip() for s in failed) or 'none'}; image job ran: {ran_image}") _ = ob.run("git checkout -q -- .", cwd=repo) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` unformatted failing steps: Format check; image job ran: False unused import failing steps: Lint; image job ran: False failing test failing steps: Tests; image job ran: False ``` ::: ::: Each defect stops `quality` at its own step — format check, lint, tests — and `image` never runs, so no image is built from a commit that fails its checks. The order of the steps is the fail-fast order of @prp-ops-stage-order. A common anti-pattern is `continue-on-error: true` on the lint step "to see all problems at once", which then lets unlinted code through. ::: ::: {#exr-ops6-gha-hard} ## Hard — a scheduled job and a cache key Add to the workflow a second trigger, `schedule` (every night at 02:17 UTC), under which a job `nightly` runs an extended test suite (marked `slow`) that does not run on pushes. Use a cache for a downloaded evaluation file, keyed by its expected SHA-256, so the file is downloaded only when the expected hash changes. Validate with actionlint and run the `nightly` job locally with act (the `schedule` event). ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Hint `if: github.event_name == 'schedule'` selects jobs by trigger; `pytest -m slow` and `-m "not slow"` split the suite. Pick an odd minute for the cron (many workflows run at :00, which delays them). The cache key can be any string — put the hash in it. ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Solution ``` {.bash} $ actionlint ``` ``` actionlint: no problems ``` ``` {.bash} $ act schedule -P ubuntu-latest=-self-hosted ``` ``` [CI/nightly ] ⭐ Run Main actions/checkout@v7 [CI/nightly ] ✅ Success - Main actions/checkout@v7 [CI/nightly ] ⭐ Run Main Install dependencies [CI/nightly ] ✅ Success - Main Install dependencies [CI/nightly ] ⭐ Run Main Extended tests | 1 passed, 5 deselected in 1.77s [CI/nightly ] ✅ Success - Main Extended tests [CI/nightly ] 🏁 Job succeeded ``` Under `schedule`, only `nightly` runs (the other jobs are skipped by their `if:`), and it runs only the slow tests; on pushes the `-m "not slow"` filter keeps them out of the fast loop. The cache key contains the expected hash of the evaluation file, so changing the file means changing the hash in the workflow, which changes the key — a cache can never serve a stale file under a new name. (The hash in the workflow is a placeholder: in a real pipeline the download step must also *verify* it, @exr-ops1-stack-hard.) Moving the session fixture into `conftest.py` was needed for two test modules to share it. ::: ## Continuous delivery and promotion gates {#sec-ops-cd} ### Separate CI from CD CD runs only for commits that passed CI, usually only on the main branch, and needs credentials that CI must not have. GitHub Actions expresses this with a separate job (or workflow) that `needs` the CI jobs, runs `if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'`, requests `packages: write` only for itself, and reads its credentials from secrets or from an **environment** with protection rules: ```yaml publish: needs: image if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' && github.event_name == 'push' runs-on: ubuntu-latest permissions: contents: read packages: write # push to the GitHub Container Registry environment: production # protection rules, environment secrets steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v7 - uses: docker/login-action@v4 with: registry: ghcr.io username: ${{ github.actor }} password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} - uses: docker/build-push-action@v7 with: push: true tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}/sentiment:${{ github.sha }} ``` The image is tagged with the **commit id**: every image can be traced to the exact code that built it (@prp-ops-commit), and a deployment refers to it by digest (@exr-ops5-rollback-digest). **Hugging Face Spaces** can host a containerised demo: a Space of type Docker is a Git repository whose `README.md` starts with a YAML header such as `sdk: docker` and `app_port: 8000`; the platform builds the Dockerfile at the root and runs it [@huggingface2026hub]. A CD job deploys by pushing the repository's files to the Space's Git remote, authenticated by a token stored as a repository secret (`HF_TOKEN`), e.g. `git push https://user:$HF_TOKEN@huggingface.co/spaces/user/sentiment main`. The build machine of this book cannot reach Hugging Face, so this step is described, not run. ### A statistical gate for models Before a retrained model (the **challenger**) replaces the one in production (the **champion**), the pipeline should check that it is not worse. Both models are evaluated on the **same** examples, so the comparison is *paired*: only the examples on which they disagree carry information. ::: {#prp-ops-mcnemar} ## McNemar's exact test On $n$ examples, let $b$ be the number the challenger gets right and the champion wrong, and $c$ the number the champion gets right and the challenger wrong. If the two models have the same accuracy on the population — more precisely, if each discordant example is equally likely to be of either kind — then, conditionally on $d = b + c$, $$ c \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(d, \tfrac12), $$ so the one-sided p-value for "the challenger is worse" is $P(X \ge c)$ with $X \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(d, \frac12)$ [@mcnemar1947]. ::: *In one line:* examples on which both models agree say nothing about which is better; among the disagreements, a fair coin decides who wins if they are equally good. ::: {.deep kind="proof"} ## Proof of @prp-ops-mcnemar Each example independently falls in one of four cells (both right, both wrong, only challenger right, only champion right) with probabilities $\pi_{11}, \pi_{00}, \pi_{10}, \pi_{01}$. The accuracies are $\pi_{11} + \pi_{10}$ and $\pi_{11} + \pi_{01}$; they are equal iff $\pi_{10} = \pi_{01}$. Given that an example is discordant, it is of the "champion right" kind with probability $\pi_{01}/(\pi_{10} + \pi_{01}) = \frac12$ under equality. The $d$ discordant examples are independent, so the number $c$ of the second kind is $\mathrm{Binomial}(d, \frac12)$ conditionally on $d$. The p-value of the observed $c$ for the alternative "champion better" is the probability of a value at least as large under the null. $\blacksquare$ ::: The test uses $d$, not $n$: two models that agree on 95 % of the examples are compared on the remaining 5 %, which is why a paired comparison detects small differences with far fewer examples than comparing two independently estimated accuracies (@exr-ops6-cd-medium). ::: {#dedae3e7 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} def mcnemar_worse(y, p_champion, p_challenger): """b, c and the one-sided exact p-value for 'the challenger is worse'.""" right_ch, right_new = p_champion == y, p_challenger == y b = int(np.sum(right_new & ~right_ch)) # challenger right, champion wrong c = int(np.sum(right_ch & ~right_new)) # champion right, challenger wrong p = binom.sf(c - 1, b + c, 0.5) if b + c else 1.0 return b, c, float(p) evaluation = ob.make_posts(4000, seed=300) y_ev = evaluation.label.to_numpy() champion = model candidates = { "retrained on a new sample": ob.train_model(ob.make_posts(3000, seed=5).text, ob.make_posts(3000, seed=5).label), "unigrams only": ob.train_model(train.text, train.label, ngram=(1, 1)), } p_champ = champion.predict(evaluation.text) for name, ch in candidates.items(): p_new = ch.predict(evaluation.text) b, c, p = mcnemar_worse(y_ev, p_champ, p_new) print(f"{name:26s} acc {np.mean(p_new == y_ev):.4f} vs {np.mean(p_champ == y_ev):.4f}; " f"b = {b:3d}, c = {c:3d}, p(worse) = {p:.2g} -> {'BLOCK' if p < 0.05 else 'pass'}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` retrained on a new sample acc 0.9237 vs 0.9217; b = 49, c = 41, p(worse) = 0.83 -> pass unigrams only acc 0.8650 vs 0.9217; b = 21, c = 248, p(worse) = 1.1e-50 -> BLOCK ``` ::: ::: The retrained model differs from the champion on about ninety posts, with no significant difference — it may be promoted (if, say, it was trained on newer data). The unigram model loses many more disagreements than it wins, and the gate blocks it. ### Practice {.unnumbered} ::: {#exr-ops6-cd-easy} ## Easy — McNemar by hand On 1 000 posts, a challenger and a champion agree on 960. Of the 40 disagreements, the challenger is right on 14 and the champion on 26. Compute the one-sided p-value for "the challenger is worse" with the binomial distribution (and its normal approximation $z = (c - b)/\sqrt{b + c}$). Would a gate at 5 % block the challenger? What do the 960 agreements contribute? ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Hint $c = 26$, $d = 40$: $P(X \ge 26)$ for $X \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(40, 0.5)$. ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Solution ::: {#f25f682f .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} b_, c_ = 14, 26 print(f"exact p = {binom.sf(c_ - 1, b_ + c_, 0.5):.4f}; normal z = {(c_ - b_) / np.sqrt(b_ + c_):.2f}, " f"p = {norm.sf((c_ - b_) / np.sqrt(b_ + c_)):.4f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` exact p = 0.0403; normal z = 1.90, p = 0.0289 ``` ::: ::: The exact p-value is about 0.04: a gate at 5 % blocks the challenger, although its accuracy (0.948 against 0.960) differs by 1.2 points only. The 960 agreements contribute nothing to the test — they would be the same whichever model is better. ::: ::: {#exr-ops6-cd-medium} ## Medium — paired versus unpaired A challenger is truly 1 point worse than the champion. By simulation (on the synthetic posts, or with binomial draws), compare how often a 5 % gate catches it with (a) McNemar's test on a shared evaluation set of $n$ posts and (b) a two-proportion test on two separate evaluation sets of $n$ posts each, for $n \in \{500, 2000, 8000\}$. Explain the difference. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Hint Model the pair of outcomes per example: with probability $\pi_{11}$ both right, $\pi_{10}$ only the champion, $\pi_{01}$ only the challenger, $\pi_{00}$ neither, chosen so that the accuracies are 0.93 and 0.92 and the models disagree on, say, 5 % of the examples. ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Solution ::: {#775b4bec .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} rng = np.random.default_rng(8) acc_old, acc_new, disagree = 0.93, 0.92, 0.05 pi10 = (disagree + (acc_old - acc_new)) / 2 # champion right only pi01 = disagree - pi10 # challenger right only pi11 = acc_old - pi10 probs = [pi11, pi10, pi01, 1 - pi11 - pi10 - pi01] for n in (500, 2000, 8000): caught_paired = caught_unpaired = 0 for _ in range(2000): cells = rng.multinomial(n, probs) b, c = cells[2], cells[1] caught_paired += (b + c) > 0 and binom.sf(c - 1, b + c, 0.5) < 0.05 k_old, k_new = rng.binomial(n, acc_old), rng.binomial(n, acc_new) pool = (k_old + k_new) / (2 * n) z = (k_old - k_new) / n / np.sqrt(2 * pool * (1 - pool) / n) caught_unpaired += norm.sf(z) < 0.05 print(f"n = {n:5d}: paired (McNemar) {caught_paired / 2000:.2f}, unpaired {caught_unpaired / 2000:.2f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` n = 500: paired (McNemar) 0.20, unpaired 0.16 n = 2000: paired (McNemar) 0.59, unpaired 0.34 n = 8000: paired (McNemar) 0.99, unpaired 0.76 ``` ::: ::: The paired test has much higher power at every size: the unpaired comparison must see a 1-point difference through the full binomial noise of two accuracies near 0.93 (variance $\approx 2 \cdot 0.93 \cdot 0.07/n$), while McNemar looks only at the 5 % of examples where the models differ, where the 1-point gap is a 30/70 split. Evaluating both models on the same examples is free — and the right design for a gate. ::: ::: {#exr-ops6-cd-hard} ## Hard — the gate in the pipeline Add to the service repository a script `gate.py` that loads the champion (`model.joblib`) and a challenger (`challenger.joblib`), evaluates both on a fixed evaluation set, prints a report and exits with status 1 when McNemar's test says the challenger is worse at the 5 % level, 0 otherwise. Add a job `gate` to the workflow that runs it, and a job `publish` that `needs` it. Run the workflow with act twice: once with a challenger retrained on a new sample, once with the unigram challenger. Show that only in the first run the `publish` job runs. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Hint `publish` can be a placeholder that prints what it would push (it needs credentials on GitHub). The evaluation set must be fixed — by seed here, by a pinned file with a hash in practice — or the gate's decision would change from run to run. ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Solution ``` {.bash} $ actionlint ``` ``` actionlint: no problems ``` **Challenger: retrained on a new sample** ``` {.bash} $ act push -P ubuntu-latest=-self-hosted ``` ``` [CI/gate ] ⭐ Run Main actions/checkout@v7 [CI/gate ] ✅ Success - Main actions/checkout@v7 [CI/gate ] ⭐ Run Main Install dependencies [CI/gate ] ✅ Success - Main Install dependencies [CI/gate ] ⭐ Run Main Challenger vs champion [CI/gate ] ✅ Success - Main Challenger vs champion [CI/gate ] 🏁 Job succeeded [CI/publish ] ⭐ Run Main echo "would push ghcr.io/nektos/act/sentiment:582354819a7e5459b6c35676efe5583c50e0b22b" [CI/publish ] ✅ Success - Main echo "would push ghcr.io/nektos/act/sentiment:582354819a7e5459b6c35676efe5583c50e0b22b" [CI/publish ] 🏁 Job succeeded ``` **Challenger: unigrams only** ``` {.bash} $ act push -P ubuntu-latest=-self-hosted ``` ``` [CI/gate ] ⭐ Run Main actions/checkout@v7 [CI/gate ] ✅ Success - Main actions/checkout@v7 [CI/gate ] ⭐ Run Main Install dependencies [CI/gate ] ✅ Success - Main Install dependencies [CI/gate ] ⭐ Run Main Challenger vs champion [CI/gate ] ❌ Failure - Main Challenger vs champion [CI/gate ] 🏁 Job failed [exit status 1] ``` With the retrained challenger the gate passes and `publish` runs; with the unigram challenger `gate.py` exits with status 1, the job fails, and `publish` — which `needs` it — never starts. The decision is reproducible because the evaluation set is fixed; its power to detect a given degradation can be planned as in @exr-ops6-cd-medium. A gate that only compares two accuracy numbers would block good challengers by chance and pass bad ones on small evaluation sets. ::: ::: {.project-link} **In the project.** The project's pipeline runs tests and style checks on every push, builds the image, and — in a separate CD part — publishes it. Follow this chapter: a `quality` job (format check, lint, tests, in the fail-fast order) and an `image` job with a smoke test of meaning, linked by `needs`; least-privilege `permissions`; a CD job restricted to the main branch whose credentials come only from secrets; images tagged by commit. Validate the workflow with actionlint before pushing. If the deployment to Hugging Face Spaces is not done, describe it as in @sec-ops-cd (Docker Space, `app_port`, token secret). When the pipeline retrains a model, gate its promotion with a paired test on a fixed evaluation set (@exr-ops6-cd-hard). ::: ## Common pitfalls ::: {.callout-warning} ## Watch out - **Long-lived branches** and integration once a week: not CI, whatever the tooling. - **Expensive stages first**, or everything sequential when it could run in parallel. - **`continue-on-error`** on checks that should block. - **Secrets in workflow files** or echoed in logs; `permissions` left at the default write access. - **Unpinned actions** (`@main`): pin at least the major version, ideally the commit. - **Rebuilding the image in CD** instead of promoting the one CI tested. - **Model gates on two accuracy numbers**: use a paired test on a fixed set. ::: ## Summary - CI integrates small changes often, each verified automatically; continuous delivery keeps every passing change releasable; continuous deployment releases it; continuous training retrains on new data. Delivery performance: deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate, time to restore. - Sequential stages in increasing $c_i/p_i$ minimise the expected cost; parallel jobs finish at the weight of the critical path. - GitHub Actions: workflows of jobs of steps; triggers, `needs`, matrices, caches keyed by lock-file hashes, least-privilege permissions, secrets, environments. actionlint checks workflows; act runs them locally. - CD: separate jobs, main branch only, images tagged by commit, credentials from secrets; Hugging Face Docker Spaces as a deployment target. - Model gates: McNemar's test uses only the disagreements, $c \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(b + c, \frac12)$ under equal accuracy, and is far more powerful than comparing two accuracies. ## Exercises ::: {#exr-ops6-noninferiority} **Non-inferiority.** A gate that blocks only *significantly* worse challengers lets through any challenger tested on too few examples. Write a **non-inferiority** gate instead: promote only if the data show, at the 5 % level, that the challenger is *not worse by more than 1 point* — using the normal approximation to the paired difference $(b - c)/n$, with variance estimated by $(b + c)/n^2 - ((b - c)/n)^2/n$. Apply it to the two challengers above with evaluation sets of 1 000 and 4 000 posts. ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Solution ::: {#b77453a3 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} def noninferior(y, p_old, p_new, margin=0.01, alpha=0.05): n = len(y) b = np.sum((p_new == y) & (p_old != y)); c = np.sum((p_old == y) & (p_new != y)) diff = (b - c) / n var = (b + c) / n**2 - diff**2 / n lower = diff - norm.ppf(1 - alpha) * np.sqrt(var) return diff, lower, lower > -margin for n in (1000, 4000): ev = ob.make_posts(n, seed=301) y = ev.label.to_numpy(); p_old = champion.predict(ev.text) for name, ch in candidates.items(): d, lo, ok = noninferior(y, p_old, ch.predict(ev.text)) print(f"n = {n}: {name:26s} difference {d:+.4f}, lower bound {lo:+.4f} -> {'promote' if ok else 'hold'}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` n = 1000: retrained on a new sample difference -0.0030, lower bound -0.0102 -> hold n = 1000: unigrams only difference -0.0860, lower bound -0.1009 -> hold n = 4000: retrained on a new sample difference +0.0010, lower bound -0.0029 -> promote n = 4000: unigrams only difference -0.0587, lower bound -0.0655 -> hold ``` ::: ::: The burden of proof is now on the challenger: with 1 000 posts the evidence may not suffice even for a good challenger (it is *held*, not promoted), whereas the "not significantly worse" gate would have let it through by default. With 4 000 posts the good challenger is shown non-inferior and the unigram model is held. Choosing between the two gates is a policy decision: non-inferiority is the safer default for automatic promotion. ::: ::: {#exr-ops6-dora} **Delivery metrics from a log.** From a list of deployments with their commit times, deployment times and whether they caused an incident (and when it was resolved), compute the four delivery metrics. Write the function and apply it to a small invented log; say which number you would try to improve first if lead time were three days and the change failure rate 30 %. ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Solution ::: {#ecf305c4 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} from datetime import datetime as dt, timedelta as td log = [ # (commit time, deploy time, incident resolved after, or None) (dt(2026, 11, 2, 9), dt(2026, 11, 5, 10), None), (dt(2026, 11, 3, 15), dt(2026, 11, 6, 11), td(hours=5)), (dt(2026, 11, 9, 10), dt(2026, 11, 12, 9), None), (dt(2026, 11, 10, 8), dt(2026, 11, 13, 16), td(hours=20)), (dt(2026, 11, 16, 11), dt(2026, 11, 19, 10), None), (dt(2026, 11, 17, 9), dt(2026, 11, 20, 15), td(hours=2)), (dt(2026, 11, 23, 14), dt(2026, 11, 26, 9), None), (dt(2026, 11, 24, 10), dt(2026, 11, 27, 12), None), (dt(2026, 11, 30, 9), dt(2026, 12, 3, 10), None), (dt(2026, 12, 1, 16), dt(2026, 12, 4, 9), None), ] days = (max(d for _, d, _ in log) - min(d for _, d, _ in log)).days lead = [d - c for c, d, _ in log] failures = [r for _, _, r in log if r is not None] print(f"deployment frequency {len(log) / days * 7:.1f} per week; median lead time " f"{sorted(lead)[len(lead) // 2]}; change failure rate {len(failures) / len(log):.0%}; " f"median time to restore {sorted(failures)[len(failures) // 2]}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` deployment frequency 2.5 per week; median lead time 3 days, 1:00:00; change failure rate 30%; median time to restore 5:00:00 ``` ::: ::: Lead times of three days with a 30 % failure rate point at large, infrequent batches: the first lever is usually to make changes smaller and the pipeline faster (CI on every change, automated tests and gates), which tends to lower the failure rate too — the observation behind @forsgren2018's finding that speed and stability improve together. ::: ## Further reading {.unnumbered} - @fowler2006 — the original description of continuous integration and its practices;
